opus-5.5.text:
I think what makes it special is really how it came together. Ivan and Aidan were working on it through For AI, which was this very scrappy, decentralized research collective. There was no single lab, no big institutional umbrella. People were spread across different cities and time zones, often contributing in their spare time, and the work moved forward through a lot of async collaboration and shared enthusiasm.

The paper looked at sparsity and pruning, at how you can train networks so they're more robust to having weights removed afterward. That question has stayed close to my heart because it connects to a bigger theme: we don't need every parameter we train, so how do we build models that are efficient by design?

But beyond the technical contribution, it was a proof of concept that you could do serious, publishable research outside the traditional pathways. For a lot of people who don't have access to a PhD program or a big industry lab, that matters enormously. It showed that if you create an open, welcoming structure where people can plug in, contribute, and get mentorship, good science can come out of it. To me that's as meaningful as the result itself. It changed what people thought was possible about who gets to participate in machine learning research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think what's special about it is really the story of how it came together, more than any single technical result. Ivan and Aidan, when they started this, were not sitting in the same lab. They weren't even on the same continent for most of it. One was finishing up a degree, the other was working on things on the side, and they essentially found each other through the Cohere For AI community, which is this open science effort we set up precisely for this kind of thing, where people who don't have a traditional research affiliation can still do serious research together.

And I think that matters because so much of what gets published in machine learning right now comes out of a very small number of institutions with very large compute budgets. The paper they produced is a counterexample to the idea that you need that to contribute. They were working with modest resources, coordinating over Discord and a shared doc, and they still ended up asking a question that I think the field had been a little bit lazy about, which is whether some of the efficiency techniques we take for granted actually hold up when you look carefully across different settings and scales.

What I found compelling about the work itself is that it's rigorous in a way that's easy to skip when you're moving fast. They didn't just report one headline number. They were careful about variance, about running multiple seeds, about being honest when the result was less clean than they'd hoped. That kind of care is what I most want to see from the community, because the field has a reproducibility problem and the cure for that is not more compute, it's more discipline.

And then the last piece, honestly, is what it did for them. Both of them have gone on to do things they probably wouldn't have had access to before, and that is the whole point. The paper is good, but the mechanism that produced it is the thing I'd really like to see replicated.
